finding: §4.2 now has TWO writers of `last_failure`, and the whole point of the second one is the claim "a gate failure the harness swallows is therefore still recorded" — `tp done` writing the record with the gate's own output as `summary`. No test in §10 exercises that writer. Test 23 pins only the driver path ("written ... on a non-zero unit exit"), so an implementation that never writes `last_failure` from `tp done` passes the entire suite while violating the section's load-bearing sentence. The swallowed-gate case (child exits 0, gate failed) is exactly the case the driver's writer cannot see, so it is untested by construction.
suggestion: Extend test 23, or add a test, asserting the `tp done` writer: with a quality gate scripted to fail and the child exiting 0, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json` exists, its `summary` carries the gate's output (not the agent's prose), and the driver did not write it.

finding: §3.5 says the driver redirects each child's stdout and stderr to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` AND substitutes that same path for `{log_path}` so "a runner that writes its own log writes to the file the driver already owns rather than a second one". Those are two independent writers of one file: the driver's redirection holds an open fd with its own offset while the runner opens the same path (typically truncating or appending with a separate offset). Test 60 pins the collision (`{log_path}` resolves to the same file the driver redirects to) rather than resolving it, and the corrupted file is exactly the one §3.2.2's spend read and the operator's post-hoc diagnosis depend on.
suggestion: Pick one owner per file. Either the driver redirects and `{log_path}` names a sibling path (`<seq>-<kind>-<id>.runner.jsonl`) the driver also records in the run-state row, or the driver does not redirect for runners that declare a log placeholder. State which, and change test 60 to assert the chosen ownership rule instead of path identity.

finding: §4.2 gives `tp done` co-ownership of `last_failure`, but the record's fields `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase}` are unit-scoped facts `tp done` can only get from the driver's child environment (`TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_PHASE`). `tp done` is a shipped command run interactively far more often than under a run, where those variables are absent. The spec never says what `tp done` writes then: skip the write entirely, write with null/empty unit fields, or synthesize a kind. Since §4.2 also makes clearing conditional on `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matching, a record written outside a run with invented ids can never be cleared by any in-run success and will be surfaced by `tp resume`/`tp brief` indefinitely.
suggestion: State the out-of-run behaviour explicitly: either `tp done` writes `last_failure` only when `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` are both present (and a bare interactive gate failure records nothing), or define the sentinel it writes (e.g. `unit_kind: "implement"`, `unit_id` = the task id, `phase` from the oracle) and state which success clears that sentinel. Add a test alongside test 23 covering a gate failure with no run environment.

finding: Test 2 says the loop "advances through implement, review and audit phases", but the cycle the oracle drives is review → decompose → implement → audit → release (§3.3's kinds and §4.1's phases), so the test names the phases out of order and omits `decompose` entirely. An engineer building the fixture cannot tell whether test 2 asserts an ordered traversal (and if so, which order) or merely that each phase was visited, and no test in §10 drives a `decompose` unit's transition at all.
suggestion: Rewrite test 2 to name the phase sequence the oracle actually reports, including `decompose`, and state explicitly whether the assertion is on order or on membership.

finding: Test 3 requires each cap to produce its own `stop_reason`, but `cap-wall-clock` has no deterministic route: §7 floors `run_max_wall_clock_seconds` at 60, §3.4 evaluates caps between iterations only, and the spec ships a runner seam (`TP_RUNNER_SEAM`) but no clock seam. A conforming test must therefore burn ≥60 s of real time, or an implementer must invent an unspecified time injection — two engineers write contradictory tests, and the slow one is the only one the spec sanctions.
suggestion: Either name a clock/elapsed seam alongside `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` (same test-only precedence), or lower the documented range floor so the cap is reachable in a unit test, and say in test 3 which mechanism the wall-clock case uses.

finding: Test 5 asserts concurrency "from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps", but the observable is not pinned and the fake runner has no specified duration. If the seam exits immediately, sibling role intervals may not overlap even under a correct parallel implementation, so the assertion fails or passes by scheduling luck; conversely an implementation that spawns roles sequentially can pass on a fast machine if the tolerance is loose. The test as written is a timing race, not a pass/fail assertion.
suggestion: Pin the observable: have the seam block until released (or sleep a specified duration) and assert that all role children of one iteration were spawned before any of them exited, and that no non-role unit's [spawn, exit] interval intersects a role unit's — a set-comparison, not a timing tolerance.

finding: Test 16 requires each §7 field to "accept both range endpoints, and reject one step outside each", but §7 declares the budget fields as decimal dollars without a precision, so "one step" is undefined for `run_max_budget_usd` (0-10000) and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` (0-1000). One engineer rejects -1 and 10001, another rejects -0.01 and 10000.01, and a third asserts 10000.005 is accepted — mutually contradictory suites, and the mutation-testing lesson in CLAUDE.md is precisely that a boundary tested with a far-away value proves nothing about inclusivity.
suggestion: Pin the decimal precision of the budget fields (e.g. two decimal places, values outside the range rejected at that granularity) and state the step test 16 uses per field type: 1 for integer fields, the pinned decimal unit for budget fields.

finding: §3.2.2 requires that a runner declaring no `spend_key` makes `run_max_budget_usd` inert "reported once at run start, not silently", and §3.2.2 further requires the run-start report to name unmetered kinds under a per-kind map. The per-unit cap gets no equivalent: §3.2.1 says the `opencode` template has "no budget flag", so a resolved non-zero `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is simply never passed to it, and nothing reports that. The operator who sets a per-unit budget under a non-`claude` template (or under a per-kind map that routes audit units to one) gets an unbounded unit with no notice — the same defect §3.2.2 fixed for the run-level cap.
suggestion: Extend the run-start report to name every resolved cap that the selected runner (per kind, under a map) cannot enforce, covering `run_max_unit_budget_usd` alongside `run_max_budget_usd`, and add the per-unit case to test 11.

finding: Spend is defined as "one number from the final line of that unit's log", but §3.5 redirects the child's stdout **and stderr** into that one file. A runner that emits any stderr line (a warning, a trailing newline flush, a harness diagnostic) after its final result line makes the last line something other than the result object, and the spec defines no behaviour for a final line that is not JSON, is JSON but lacks `spend_key`, or is a truncated write from a killed child. The implementer must invent a policy (scan backwards for the last parseable object? treat as null? fail the unit?), and that policy decides whether `cap-budget` silently stops accruing.
suggestion: Pin the read rule: scan the log backwards for the last line that parses as JSON and contains `spend_key`, take that value, and report `spend: null` when no such line exists — never a unit failure. State that a null spend on a runner that declares a `spend_key` is reported (not silently zero) so the operator sees a partial total, mirroring §3.2.2's unmetered-kind report.

finding: §3.2.2 reads spend from "the final line of that unit's log", but §3.5 mandates that the log is stdout AND stderr merged into one file. Any stderr write that lands after the runner's final result object — a harness warning, a shell diagnostic, a plugin hook's stderr (§6.2/§6.4 hooks run inside the child) — makes the last line a non-JSON line, so spend silently reads as null and `cap-budget` silently stops accruing. The design treats a null spend as "this runner declares no spend_key" (a configuration fact), so the failure is indistinguishable from the supported case.
suggestion: Define the read as "the last line that parses as JSON and contains the configured key, scanning backwards", and distinguish "runner declares no spend_key" (spend null, reported at run start) from "declared key not found in this unit's log" (a reported anomaly). Alternatively keep stderr in a separate file so the result stream stays clean, and say so in §3.5.

finding: `A unit is attempted 1 + run_max_unit_retries times` never says where the attempt counter lives or when a retry runs. §3.5 forbids any decision from reading the run state back, so the counter must be in-driver memory — yet §3.1 says the driver never holds work it could re-derive, and §3.1's loop re-polls the oracle every iteration, which would return the same unit again as an ordinary next unit. Whether a retry is an immediate respawn inside the same iteration (skipping the oracle re-poll) or a fresh iteration, and whether the counter is keyed by `(kind, id)` or by position, changes `totals.units`, the `cap-units` arithmetic, and what §3.1.1's "delete the role file before spawning" applies to on attempt 2.
suggestion: State that the driver keeps a per-run, in-memory attempt count keyed by `(kind, id)`, that a retry is spawned immediately within the same iteration without re-polling the oracle, that each attempt appends its own run-state row with an incremented `attempt` and a fresh log path, and that the counter resets on a new run (matching test 6's crash-resume behaviour).

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1.1 defines an `audit-fix` unit's id as the finding's `role:item_id`. `item_id` is authored by an audit sub-agent, so it can carry `/`, spaces, `:`, unicode, or hundreds of characters — none of which the spec constrains. `{log_path}` is also interpolated into the runner's argv (§3.2.1), and the same id reaches `TP_UNIT_ID`, so an id containing `/` either creates an unintended subdirectory or fails the open. No sanitization, length cap, or id validation is stated anywhere.
suggestion: Define a filename-safe transform for the id component of the log path (e.g. replace every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` with `-`, truncate to N characters and append a short hash of the full id), state that `TP_UNIT_ID` still carries the untransformed id, and add it to test 60's assertion that `{log_path}` equals the redirect target.

finding: `tp resume --json` now emits the same unit twice: `next_units[0]` carries {kind, id, brief_command}, and `next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` are defined to render that same entry. §4.1 also states the driver parses `next_units`, `round` and `phase` and nothing else — so on the machine path `next_action` is pure duplication of bytes in the payload every iteration parses, and §7's only `--compact` rule covers run state, saying nothing about which of the two survives compaction.
suggestion: State the compaction/emission split explicitly in §4.1: under `--compact` (and whenever `next_units` is non-empty) emit `next_action` as `summary` only, dropping `command`/`brief_command`/`payload` since they are recoverable from `next_units[0]`; keep the full human-facing object in TTY/non-compact output. Add a test asserting the compact payload carries each brief_command exactly once.

finding: §3.1.1 assigns the derivation of `$TP_ROUND_DIR` (`.tp/rounds/<base>/$TP_PHASE-r$TP_ROUND`) to the driver, which "substitutes" `round` and `phase` into it (§4.1). But §4.1 also requires the oracle to omit "any role whose findings file already satisfies §3.3's predicate" — which means `tp resume` must itself locate `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r<round>/role-<id>.ndjson`. The spec never says the oracle owns or emits that path, so two components independently derive one path from the same three inputs; a change to the layout in one drifts the other silently, which is the second-source-of-truth failure §3.5 names as the postmortem's central drift.
suggestion: Have `tp resume --json` emit `round_dir` (absolute) next to `round` and `phase`, and state that the driver uses that value verbatim for `TP_ROUND_DIR` rather than recomputing it — keeping §4.1's "whole machine surface" explicit at four keys. Extend test 37 to assert `TP_ROUND_DIR` equals the oracle's emitted `round_dir`.

finding: The `tp done` writer must stamp `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code}`, but §4.2 never says where those values come from for that writer, nor what it does when they are unavailable. Inside a run they presumably come from `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_PHASE`, but `tp done` is also run interactively with those unset — one engineer writes empty strings, another omits the fields, a third skips the write entirely, and all three claim conformance. `exit_code` is equally unpinned for this writer: the gate's exit code or `tp done`'s own. Because a success clears the record only when `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matches, an unpinned stamp makes the clearing rule itself untestable — a record written with an empty key can never be cleared.
suggestion: State that `tp done` takes `unit_kind`/`unit_id`/`phase` from `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_PHASE`, name the value used when they are unset (e.g. omit the write entirely outside a run, mirroring `tp escalate`'s rule), and pin `exit_code` to the gate's exit code for this writer.

finding: The round-16 repair names two writers but keeps the unchanged rule "a second failure overwrites it", with no precedence between them. In the ordinary in-run case both fire for one event: `tp done` writes the record with the gate's own output, the child then exits non-zero and the driver overwrites it with the coarser {failing command, log path}. Last-writer-wins therefore discards the gate output in exactly the case the second writer was introduced to preserve; only the swallowed-exit-code case keeps it.
suggestion: State the precedence explicitly in §4.2: the driver's write does not overwrite a `last_failure` already written for the same `(unit_kind, unit_id)` during the same attempt (or the driver merges its log path into the existing record rather than replacing it). Add an invariant in §10.6 that a gate failure inside a unit leaves the gate output as `summary`, not the driver's command line.

finding: `tp done` is not a run-only command, but the object it must now write is keyed on `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase}` — values that exist only as `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_PHASE` in a driver-spawned child (§3.1.1). The repair does not say what `tp done` writes when a gate fails outside a run, so the identity fields are undefined, and the clear rule ("a success clears it only when `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matches") has no defined behaviour for records written with absent identity — including whether a later manual success clears them at all.
suggestion: Say in §4.2 whether `tp done` writes `last_failure` outside a run. Either fence the writer to a unit context (write only when `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` are set, otherwise no record), or define the out-of-run identity and its clear semantics; add the chosen behaviour to §10.3 item 23.

finding: §4.2 names `tp done` as one of the two `last_failure` writers and defines the record as `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code, summary, at}`, with clearing gated on `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matching. But `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` exist only for children the driver spawns (§3.1.1, "applied on the same terms as `TP_UNATTENDED`"), and `tp done` is the command operators run interactively every cycle. The spec does not say what an out-of-run `tp done` writes for those two fields, nor whether an out-of-run success can clear a driver-written record — so a hand-run gate failure either writes an unidentifiable record or none, and an interactive success may or may not clear the record that `tp resume`/`tp brief` keep surfacing. §5.2 sets the precedent for this case (`tp escalate` outside a run is a usage error) and §4.2 sets no rule at all.
suggestion: Say explicitly what `tp done` does when `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` are unset: either write `unit_kind: "implement"` with the task id as `unit_id` (so an in-run and an out-of-run close produce the same key and clear each other) or skip the write entirely outside a run. Add the interactive case to test 23.

finding: §5.1 fences `runner` and `notify_cmd` so "a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer", but §7 says `notify_cmd` resolves from `.tp/local.json` only. `tp set --workflow` writes the task file, so refusing `notify_cmd` there fences a layer the field never resolves from, while the layer it does resolve from has no named tp command — leaving the implementer unsure whether a command to write `.tp/local.json` defaults exists and must be fenced, and §6.2's `PreToolUse` deny (which does cover `.tp/local.json`) is described as anti-hand-editing rather than as this fence's enforcement point.
suggestion: Name the write path for each fenced field and fence it there: state which command mutates `.tp/local.json` defaults (or that none exists and the hook deny in §6.2 is the whole enforcement for `notify_cmd`), and say the same for `runner`'s CLI/task-override layers. Extend test 40 to assert the refusal at the layer each field actually resolves from.

finding: §6.3 requires the reviewer and auditor agents to "write exactly one path … and [be] denied every other write", then states that "the definitions carry tool restrictions only". A tool restriction is per-tool, not per-path: allowing the write tool at all permits every path, and denying it blocks the required findings file. The spec names no mechanism at the granularity the requirement (and test 55) needs, while §6.2 solves the identical problem for the fence with a path-matching `PreToolUse` hook. An implementer has to guess between an agent-level permission rule, a second hook, or a weaker tool-level approximation.
suggestion: Name the mechanism explicitly. Either express the allowlist as path-scoped permission rules in the agent definition (and show the rule form), or fold role-unit write scoping into the existing `PreToolUse` hook (deny every Write/Edit outside `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` when `TP_UNIT_KIND` ends in `-role`), and restate test 55 against whichever artifact actually carries it.

finding: §6.3 states the reviewer and auditor "may write exactly one path ... and are denied every other write", and test 55 asserts "deny every other path". A role unit's whole job is to run `tp review`/`tp audit` and, on escalation, `tp escalate` — all shell invocations — so the agent must hold a shell tool, and §6.2 says explicitly that "Shell tools are deliberately outside the matcher: the denial exists to stop hand-editing, not to sandbox", while §5.1 concedes that "a unit that ... edits a config file through a shell is outside what tp can prevent". The absolute claim in §6.3 therefore contradicts the two sections that define the enforcement boundary, and test 55 as written asserts a guarantee the design disclaims.
suggestion: Scope §6.3's claim the way §6.2 scopes its own: "deny every other path to the file-writing tools (Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit); shell-mediated writes are out of scope on the same terms as §6.2". Restate test 55 over the file-writing tool set only.

finding: §7 gives `notify_cmd` a single resolution source — `.tp/local.json` only, per-operator, git-ignored — and in the same section says `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields "on the same terms as every existing workflow field". Those two sentences cannot both hold: `tp config --extract` lifts task-file workflow overrides into the committed `.tp/config.json`, a layer `notify_cmd` never reads, so extraction is either a silent no-op or it publishes a per-operator command into a committed file. §5.1 compounds it by fencing `notify_cmd` so a unit "cannot set them at all, at any layer", and test 40 asserts that — implying set paths (task override, CLI, env) that §7 says do not resolve, so a `tp set --workflow notify_cmd=` outside unattended mode writes a value that nothing ever reads.
suggestion: State explicitly in §7 that `notify_cmd` is not a layered workflow field: `--extract` skips it, `validate --project` rejects it in `.tp/config.json` and in a task-file override, and `tp set --workflow notify_cmd=` is a usage error at every layer (which also makes §5.1's fence for it vacuous by construction rather than by enforcement). Reword test 40 accordingly.

finding: `location_clusters` is added to both `tp review --merge` and `--status`, is explicitly "reporting only" (no arithmetic, no `clean` flag, no `--status --check` exit-code effect), and its own motivating measurement is 63 findings sharing a location — so the array can approach one entry per finding, with `roles[]` and `severities[]` per entry. Nothing in the driver branches on it (§3.1 reads exit codes and disk state), so on every round the `review-record` unit parses a block that feeds no decision it makes, and §8a.1 gives it no `--compact` disposition.
suggestion: Scope the emission to where it is read: carry `location_clusters` in `--status` (the operator-facing stop report, alongside the divergence signals §3.5 already surfaces) and strip it under `--compact` on `--merge`, or emit only clusters above a stated size. State the `--compact` rule for it in §8a.1 the way §7 does for run state, and assert it in test 28.

finding: `location_clusters` is specified for `tp review --merge` **and** `--status`, but only `--merge` has an obvious input set. `--status` reports across rounds, and the spec never says which findings it clusters — the last recorded round, the current round's role files, or every round — nor whether the entry set is recomputed at read time or stored with the round when `--record` runs. §8a.4 by contrast explicitly extends its change to both merges; §8a.1 says nothing about `tp audit --merge`, so it is unclear whether the omission is deliberate.
suggestion: State the `--status` input set (e.g. the most recently recorded round's merged findings, recomputed at read time and never stored, so Non-Goal 4 and the `clean` flag are untouched) and say explicitly whether `tp audit --merge`/`--status` gain `location_clusters` or are out of scope. Extend test 28 to pin the `--status` source.

finding: Test 15 asserts four paths are git-ignored by the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` and §10.7 says the fixture "gains four entries", but two of the four paths are templated on the task-file base (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) and the spec never gives the literal ignore patterns. A fixture assertion needs the exact text: `run-*.json` vs `/run-*.json` vs a per-base line are all defensible readings, and the last one is not even expressible in a static shipped file.
suggestion: List the four literal `.tp/.gitignore` lines in §3.5 (or §10.2 test 15) so the fixture assertion has one right answer.

finding: Test item 23 still describes a single writer — `last_failure` "is written ... on a non-zero unit exit" — so nothing in §10 covers the writer the round-16 repair added, nor its stated justification ("a gate failure the harness swallows is therefore still recorded"). The unchanged test list now under-covers the changed section.
suggestion: Extend §10.3 item 23 (or add an item) so the `tp done` writer is asserted: a failed gate whose non-zero exit is swallowed by the harness still leaves `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json` with the gate output as `summary`.

finding: Test 26 requires the Stop hook to "never fire for a non-role kind", but §6.2 registers the hook on the `Stop` event unconditionally and describes it as firing and then applying the predicate when `TP_UNIT_KIND` ends in `-role`. So the hook process does run for every kind; only the block is conditional. One engineer asserts the hook was not invoked (fails a conforming implementation), another asserts it did not block (passes).
suggestion: Reword test 26 to "never blocks for a non-role kind", and state in §6.2 whether the hook is expected to be invoked-and-exit-allow or matcher-scoped so it is never invoked.

finding: §3.1 step 4 says "Spawn a runner process per unit — units marked concurrent together", which reads as a per-entry mark carried in `next_units`. §4.1 rules that out in terms: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table", and pins the machine surface at `next_units`, `round` and `phase`. An implementer reading §3.1 first will add a concurrency field to the oracle's payload and break §4.1's surface contract.
suggestion: Reword step 4 as "units whose kind §3.3 marks concurrent together, every other kind alone" so the source of the concurrency decision is unambiguous at both sites.

finding: Nine variables are exported to every child, but `TP_ROUND` names no consumer anywhere in the spec once `TP_ROUND_DIR` is also exported: the round number's only stated use is deriving `TP_ROUND_DIR` (which the driver does), the escalation record's fields are {decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at} with no round, and the Stop hook (§6.2) reads `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_ROUND_DIR` and `TP_RUN_DIR`/`TP_UNIT_SEQ`. Each exported name is contract the plugin, the hooks, the docs and test 37 must all carry.
suggestion: Either name the consumer of `TP_ROUND` in §3.1.1 (e.g. a brief or hook that needs the bare number rather than the path), or drop it and keep `TP_ROUND_DIR` as the single round-scoped variable — adjusting §3.1.1's unset-not-empty rule and test 37/46 to the remaining name.

finding: Caps are "evaluated between iterations only", and the overshoot sentence covers wall-clock and budget but not units. An iteration that spawns N concurrent role units can therefore push spawned children well past `run_max_units` before the next check — with a 5-role corpus and a cap 2 short, the run spawns 5 more. Whether `run_max_units` is a pre-spawn admission check (spawn only as many as remain) or a purely post-iteration observation is left to the implementer, and the two produce different `totals.units` for test 33's arithmetic.
suggestion: State which it is. Either add `run_max_units` to the overshoot sentence ("a run can overshoot its unit, wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration"), or make it a pre-spawn admission check and say the iteration is truncated rather than partially spawned. Assert the chosen behaviour in test 3 for a concurrent role iteration.

finding: `file_summary` gains two keys where one carries the information: with `total_changed` (pre-cap count) and `total_files` (audited count) both in the payload, `truncated` is exactly `total_changed > total_files`. The justification given — that the flag is in the payload so `--quiet` cannot erase it — applies identically to `total_changed`, so it does not earn the second key; every auditor and driver now parses a bool it could compute.
suggestion: Either drop `truncated` and define the truncation condition as `total_changed > total_files` (updating test 30 to assert the two numbers), or keep the bool and justify it as the stable key drivers branch on, saying so in §8a.3 so the redundancy is a deliberate contract rather than an accident.

finding: §8a.5 justifies the arity change with "Every command's `Args` validator exits 2, matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is Non-Goals and contains no definition of a usage error or any exit-code statement; the exit-code contract in this spec lives in §3.4 (and in tp's standing 0/1/2/3/4 table). An implementer following the reference lands on the wrong section.
suggestion: Point the sentence at §3.4 (or at the standing exit-code table in `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`) instead of §9.

finding: Non-Goal 5 states "Read-only role units fan out", but §3.3 defines a role unit's whole purpose as a durable write (`$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`) and §6.3 grants the reviewer/auditor agents exactly that write path. §3.3 carries the accurate qualifier — "read-only with respect to shared state" — and the Non-Goal drops it, so the one sentence a reader is most likely to quote back states something the design contradicts three sections earlier.
suggestion: Restate Non-Goal 5 as "No parallel writing to shared state. Role units, which write only their own findings file, fan out; anything that writes shared state runs alone."
